passage.title: Should Children Be Punished Like Adults?
paras: In England and Wales, a child can be charged with a crime from the age of ten. Most young people who are charged are dealt with in youth courts, which are less formal than adult courts and aim to stop them offending again. Some people think this is too soft. Others think it is still too harsh. Who is right?

The case for treating children like adults. Supporters say that a crime is a crime, whoever commits it. A victim who has been hurt or robbed suffers just as much whether the offender is fifteen or fifty. They argue that firm punishment deters others, and that teenagers know the difference between right and wrong.

The case against. Opponents point out that children's brains are still developing, especially the parts that control impulses and judge risks. Many young offenders have difficult lives at home, have been in care or have missed school. Locking them up with adult criminals may teach them more crime. They argue that help, education and making amends to the victim work better.
Different countries draw the line in different places. Scotland raised its age of criminal responsibility from eight to twelve in 2021.
What seems clear is that justice for young people must do two things at once: take the harm to victims seriously, and give children a real chance to change.
